title: Crusoe abandons $1.25B plan to use Boom turbines at AI data centers
content:
Crusoe, a Denver-based AI data center startup that recently raised $3.9 billion, has ended plans to use a new line of stationary power plants developed by fellow Denver company Boom Supersonic.
Founded in 2018 as a bitcoin miner that ran on excess natural gas from oil fields, Crusoe has since become one of the biggest builders of AI data centers, including a massive campus in Abilene, Texas, that supplies computing power to OpenAI.
Boom Supersonic, which is developing a supersonic passenger jet called Overture, launched a new business last year to sell a version of the engine it’s developing for that jet as natural gas-fired stationary power plants. Its Superpower turbine shares about 80% of the same parts with that airborne engine, called Symphony.
Crusoe had signed on to be the first customer for this business, agreeing to spend $1.25 billion on 29 of Boom’s 42-megawatt Superpower turbines. The first deliveries were supposed to begin in 2027. But that deal has since fallen apart, according to Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl.
Friday, in a post on X, after congratulating Crusoe founders Cully Cavness and Chase Lochmiller on the company’s recent raise, Scholl said the companies are no longer moving forward with the turbine launch partnership. Although he did note that other customers were in its pipeline.
“The TL/DR is that turbines are no longer part of Crusoe’s near term primary power mix at Abilene/etc., so a launch partnership just didn’t make sense,” he wrote in the post. “Boom will be delivering about 250MW of Superpowers next year to other sites, and we’re targeting 1GW in 2028. We’re grateful for the help Crusoe gave us in shaping Superpower and continue cheering for their successes. The future is long, and we look forward to potentially teaming up if/when turbines become part of their primary power mix.”
Crusoe confirmed to TechCrunch that it is no longer doing business with Boom.
“We build AI factories from the power up, and we’re bringing new campuses online across the country, powered by innovative energy sources,” spokesperson Andrew Schmitt said in an email. “As our portfolio grows, we stay flexible, choosing the energy solutions that are right for each site as its needs evolve — including turbines, along with wind, solar, batteries and the grid. While Boom has been a great partner, the partnership isn’t the right fit today. We wish them well.”
Crusoe’s initial 1.2 gigawatt data center in Abilene that was built for Oracle and OpenAI is powered by the grid, according to the company. There is also a gas-turbine power plant that is used for backup power only. Crusoe is also building a 900 megawatt data center in Abilene for Microsoft, which will be powered by on-site gas turbines.
Losing its launch customer is seemingly a setback for Boom, which raised $300 million last year, largely to commercialize the new business. The idea, Scholl told TechCrunch at the time, was to use profits from the stationary power plant business to fund the development of Overture.
Scholl could not be reached for comment before publication; TechCrunch will update this article if he responds.

report.summary: Crusoe cancels its $1.25 billion order for 29 Boom Supersonic gas turbines, dropping the startup as launch customer for AI data center power.
report.background: AI data centers are straining global power systems, pushing developers to secure generation far beyond grid interconnection queues. Crusoe, founded in 2018 as a bitcoin miner using stranded natural gas, has become a major AI data center builder, including a 1.2 GW Abilene, Texas campus for Oracle and OpenAI. Boom Supersonic, known for the Overture supersonic jet, launched a stationary power business selling Superpower turbines — roughly 80% shared parts with its Symphony jet engine — to help fund Overture's development. Crusoe became the launch customer with a $1.25 billion, 29-turbine order for 2027 delivery. The deal reflected a broader scramble for gas turbines, whose major manufacturers are sold out into the late 2020s, as AI campuses seek reliable on-site power.
key_points: Crusoe has pulled out of its $1.25 billion agreement to buy 29 of Boom Supersonic's 42-megawatt Superpower gas turbines, a deal that would have made it the launch customer for Boom's stationary power business. Boom CEO Blake Scholl announced the split on X; Crusoe confirmed it is no longer doing business with Boom, calling it a portfolio fit issue rather than a technology failure.

Crusoe's Abilene strategy shows its evolving power mix: the 1.2 GW OpenAI/Oracle campus runs on grid power with a gas turbine only for backup, while a new 900 MW Microsoft campus will use on-site gas turbines. The company says it now chooses among turbines, wind, solar, batteries and grid on a site-by-site basis as needs change.

Boom says the cancellation does not kill Superpower. It expects to deliver about 250 MW of turbines next year to other customers and targets 1 GW in 2028. The company raised $300 million last year largely to commercialize the business, which is meant to fund development of its Overture supersonic passenger jet.

The reversal highlights a mismatch in timelines and scale: Boom's first deliveries were not due until 2027, while AI data center power demand is immediate. Crusoe, which recently raised $3.9 billion, can secure existing turbine suppliers and grid contracts faster, leaving Boom to prove its turbine can win non-launch customers on price and delivery.
report.impact: Power procurement is now the defining constraint on AI expansion. Losing its launch customer is a real setback for Boom, whose stationary turbine business was meant to bankroll Overture; it must now sell Superpower without a marquee AI data center reference. For the AI industry, the episode underscores that data center builders will abandon even ambitious energy bets if timelines or economics shift, favoring proven turbines and grid deals. Developers may face tighter gas turbine availability and should hedge with multiple power strategies. For regular users, the outcome could affect how quickly new AI capacity comes online, influencing cloud prices and energy costs, while continued reliance on gas turbines at campuses raises local emissions and grid-strain concerns.
report.tools: To follow power and data center trends: Electricity Maps and WattTime APIs track grid carbon intensity; NREL's ReEDS and PyPSA model generation portfolios; PowerGenome builds power system inputs. For data center tracking, Data Center Map and SemiAnalysis offer capacity updates. Boom Supersonic's Superpower page and GE Vernova/Siemens Energy turbine backlogs are worth watching. Open-source energy dashboards like OpenNEM show regional grid dynamics. These help assess whether AI campuses can secure on-site generation.
